paras: The lynching of Ed Roach was the killing of a Black laborer by a mob that took him from the Person County jail near Roxboro, North Carolina, in late July 1920, after he was charged with attempting to assault a white girl. Soon afterward his white employer, the contractor Nello Teer, published a letter stating that Roach had been at work when the crime was committed. The case drew editorial comment across the country as a lynching of an innocent man, and Governor Bickett offered rewards for the arrest of each member of the mob.

According to Teer, Roach had worked for him off and on for two years and on the job near Mount Tersa station since November 1, 1919. On a Monday Roach told Teer he was sick and wanted to see a doctor, and Teer arranged for him to go to Roxboro on Tuesday night. Teer also wrote that a stranger "about Ed. Roach's size," hired at his camp that Monday, left his team on Tuesday morning and ran from the foreman about three-quarters of a mile from the scene of the crime.

The crime for which Roach was lynched was put between 2 and 3 o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, while, by Teer's account, Roach stayed at work until about 5:30. He then walked to Mount Tersa station, followed by two men searching for the suspect, rode the train to Roxboro and was arrested as he got off. Teer, citing the chief of police and the sheriff, wrote that Roach denied the charge, told the girl when she was brought to the jail that she was mistaken, and was refused permission to see Teer's superintendent.

A mob then took Roach from the Person County jail and killed him. The Greenville (S.C.) News wrote that he was "hurriedly lynched" and given no opportunity to clear himself. Governor Coolidge's statement, as printed in the Iowa Bystander, said he was burned at the stake, a detail no other account in the coverage gives.

After reading the Durham Herald's editorials on the lynching, Teer wrote to that paper that "an innocent man was murdered." The Tulsa Star reported that Governor Thomas W. Bickett "promptly offered the largest reward legally permissible" for each member of the mob. No report of arrests, an inquest or indictments of mob members appears in the coverage.

In mid-August, on an appeal from the New England Society for the Prevention of Lynchings, Governor Coolidge issued a statement scoring the lynching and the Paris, Texas, burnings as disgraces and urging Congress to pass the anti-lynching bill.

White papers took up the case in editorials rather than news reports, and those found name neither the victim nor the town. A Houston Post editorial, reprinted in Wilmington on August 3 under "Hang the Lynchers," said a North Carolina jury "ought to hang a few lynchers," and the Bemidji Daily Pioneer called the victim "an innocent and law-abiding man." Late in August the Norwich Bulletin quoted the Greenville News, which named Roxboro, reported that the North Carolina press was "seething," cited the Charlotte Observer's claim that the state's honor was at stake, and concluded that the mob "murdered justice."

The Black press gave the employer's account in his own words: on August 7 the Tulsa Star ran Teer's letter in full from an Associated Negro Press dispatch under the headline "Durham Atrocity Victim Declared Innocent." The same issue's editorial contrasted Bickett's response, and his use of machine guns to protect prisoners at Graham a week later, with Texas's response to Paris. The Cleveland Advocate reprinted a Washington Star editorial that cited the case as a lynching "upon mere suspicion," and the Iowa Bystander printed Coolidge's statement that the man was lynched because "he was black."

The victim's name is printed as "Ed. Roach" in Teer's letter and as "Ed Reach" in the Coolidge brief, which also spells the county "Pearson." Only Coolidge's statement says he was burned at the stake, while Teer's letter and the other accounts say only that he was lynched; the accuser is a 14-year-old girl in Coolidge's statement and a white woman in the Greenville News.

accounts.label: Employer's letter (Nello Teer)
accounts.gist: Roach worked until about 5:30 on the Tuesday of the crime, put at 2-3 p.m., then took the train to Roxboro to see a doctor and was arrested on arrival; a stranger who fled the camp that morning near the scene was the likelier suspect.

accounts.label: Tulsa Star editorial
accounts.gist: A Negro charged with assaulting a white girl was taken from the Person County jail and lynched; his employer showed the next day he was innocent, and Governor Bickett offered rewards for the mob.

accounts.label: Governor Coolidge's statement
accounts.gist: Ed Reach, taken from the Person County jail, was burned at the stake on a charge of attacking a 14-year-old white girl; his employer furnished an alibi after the mob finished.

accounts.label: Greenville (S.C.) News editorial
accounts.gist: A Negro was seized by a mob at Roxboro and hurriedly lynched on a charge of attempted assault on a white woman, with no chance to clear himself; a contractor's statement shows he was at work.

accounts.label: Unattributed editorial notices
accounts.gist: A North Carolina mob lynched a Negro later shown by his white employer to be innocent.

framing.detail: Tulsa Star headlined the A.N.P. dispatch 'DURHAM ATROCITY VICTIM DECLARED INNOCENT' and 'Such Horrors Are Likely to Arouse Protesting American Sentiment'.
Tulsa Star editorial set the lynching beside Bickett's defense of prisoners at Graham to praise him as a governor who does his duty, against Texas's Governor Hobby.
Iowa Bystander printed Coolidge's statement that the man was killed because 'he was black' and called for the anti-lynching bill.
Cleveland Advocate reprinted a Washington Star editorial citing the case as a lynching 'upon mere suspicion'.
Houston Post editorial, reprinted in Wilmington under 'Hang the Lynchers', called for a North Carolina jury to hang the lynchers.
Bemidji Daily Pioneer called the victim 'an innocent and law-abiding man' and compared mob violence at home to attacks on Americans abroad.
Norwich Bulletin quoted the Greenville News: 'the mob not only murdered a man but it murdered justice'.

conflicts.note: Roach appears repeatedly in the employer's own letter; Reach appears once in a garbled brief and is likely a misprint.
Only Governor Coolidge's statement, made outside the state, says he was burned; the employer's letter and the other editorials do not describe how he was killed.
The employer's letter calls her 'the little girl'.

record_check.dossier: Not supported: the alleged crime was on a Tuesday and the lynching followed; the first editorial comment ran 1920-08-03 and Teer's letter was reported from Durham on Aug. 5, so the lynching was in late July 1920 (exact date not stated). Aug. 11-12 is only the date of Coolidge's statement.
Ed. Roach in the employer's letter; 'Ed Reach' only in the Coolidge brief

record_check.record: said to have committed a crime (suspicion only)
record_check.dossier: Arrested, jailed and charged with attempted criminal assault on a white girl; the 'mere suspicion' wording is a Washington Star characterization
Lynched 'near Roxboro'; seized at Roxboro from the Person County jail; the alleged crime was near Mount Tersa station on Teer's work

record_check.record: charged with attacking a 14-year-old white girl
record_check.dossier: Supported (attempted criminal assault on a white girl, 14 in Coolidge's statement)
Supported; Coolidge's statement alone adds burning at the stake

record_check.record: A mob seized a Black man at Roxboro ... A white contractor later testified he was at work
record_check.dossier: Supported, but the contractor's account was a published letter to the Durham Herald, not testimony; it should name him Ed Roach and Nello Teer

info: Alleged crime on a Tuesday between 2 and 3 p.m.; Roach arrested that evening at Roxboro; date of the lynching not stated, but before 1920-08-03 (first editorial comment); Coolidge's statement says 'just Wednesday'
Near Roxboro, Person County; seized at Roxboro after being held in the Person County jail
Ed. Roach (Teer's letter); 'Ed Reach' (Coolidge statement); a Black laborer employed by contractor Nello Teer
Attempted criminal assault on a white girl, described as 14 years old; Greenville News says a white woman

sources.note: A.N.P. dispatch, Durham, Aug. 5: contractor Nello Teer's letter to the Durham Herald declares Ed. Roach, lynched near Roxboro, Person County, innocent; Roach worked until about 5:30 Tuesday, crime at 2-3 p.m.
quotes: declares that Roach was innocent of the attempted crime, that he could not possibly have been guilty, and that the mob made a ghastly mistake in killing Roach.
When this Negro was lynched an innocent man was murdered as would have been had you or I been the victim of the mob.

sources.note: Continuation of Teer's letter (printed under a photo caption): Roach followed to Mount Tersa station by two searchers, arrested on leaving the train at Roxboro, denied the charge, request to see superintendent refused.
quotes: He dented it and told the little girl when she was brought in that she was mistaken

sources.note: Continuation of Teer's letter: a strange Negro of Roach's size and dress fled the camp Tuesday morning near the scene; Teer says circumstances point to him.
quotes: He was a strange Negro who had never been in any of our camps before, and the circumstances would point to him as the guilty party.
